A 50-minute lesson in five steps

Built on two examples, “Europe on 27 June 1914” and “Europe on 1 July 1920”. Any pair of examples works the same way.

  1. Before class (5 min)

    Open the first example on the classroom screen and check that it loads. Copy its link for the students.

  2. Introduce (10 min)

    Show Europe on 27 June 1914 and read the question under it together.

  3. Explore in pairs (15 min)

    Students open both examples on their own devices and list what changed between 1914 and 1920.

  4. Discuss (15 min)

    Collect the changes. Which empires lost land, and which states appeared?

  5. Wrap up (5 min)

    Each pair moves the clock (the button at the bottom right of the map) to a year of its choice and reports one change. The Share button turns their view into a link you can collect.

Nothing in this lesson needs an account. A teacher who signs in can also ask Atlas questions in words; Atlas has a daily limit per account.

Classroom tours

A tour is a short lesson already laid out: a few maps in order, each with sentences to read out and a question for the class. It opens full screen in the map — large type for a projector, everything else put away — and you move through it with Next and Previous.

Europe before and after the First World War, 1914–1920

Three dates on one map of Europe: the eve of the war, the armistice, and the map after the peace treaties.

Where the examples fit Japan’s high-school course

For teachers in Japan: the 2018 Course of Study for upper secondary school made Geography (地理総合) and History (歴史総合) compulsory for every student. The headings below are quoted from it; which example fits which heading is IntMap’s own suggestion, not an official one.

Section of the Course of StudyExamples
Geography (Chiri Sōgō) B (1) Diversity of ways of life and international understandingClimates of the world (Köppen–Geiger)
Geography (Chiri Sōgō) C (1) The natural environment and disaster preventionVolcanoes and plate boundaries
History (Rekishi Sōgō) B Modernisation and usJapan in 1900
History (Rekishi Sōgō) C Changes in the international order, mass society and usEurope on 27 June 1914
Europe on 1 July 1920
History (Rekishi Sōgō) D Globalisation and usCold War Europe, 1985

Source: Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, “高等学校学習指導要領（平成30年告示）”, read on 1 October 2026. The Course of Study (PDF, mext.go.jp) ↗

Sources and reliability

Every provider is named

The Data sources page lists every organisation whose data the map shows, with its licence.

Data sources →

Past dates are drawn only from what describes them

Set the clock to a date and a layer whose source does not describe that date is not drawn. The map lists what it is leaving out, so students are never shown today’s data under an old date.

Where the borders come from

Before 1689: 54 snapshots from the historical-basemaps project, each one a single year, so a border between two snapshots is an approximation. 1689–1885: OpenHistoricalMap. 1886–2019: CShapes 2.0, day by day. The base map’s coastlines are today’s.

How the numbers are worked out

Every calculation and simulation, with its assumptions, is explained on the Science & logic page.
